column2: Visit of John Cage and Merce Cunningham: a demonstration by Cunningham; Cage plays sixteen sonatas and four interludes (Sonatas and Interludes) and talks about his music (“in time than in harmonics”); the students pile presents under their car; an invitation for the summer
Faculty meeting (1948 summer session); Isaac Rosenfeld to Levi (March 18, April 15), recommended by Hannah Arendt (April 12) and Kazin (April 13)
Cunningham to the Alberses; Lippold to Albers (May 24: the hearse); Cage's night letter to Dreier and Albers (June 17, 1948: “tested their hearse for sleeping purposes”)
Faculty meetings of June 7 and 8, 1948 on the salary scale

Special faculty meeting just before the summer: the Board deadlocks on Levi's proposals (new faculty, an enlarged Board) and refuses a trip to Chicago; a vote won by one vote is reconsidered and reversed in the absence of Levi's supporters (Perrow); Levi resigns the rectorship; the Levis are granted a year's leave
Donald Droll (19, Valley Forge Military Academy) arrives among some forty new students at the end of June 1948; he stays the following year
Special meeting of the regular faculty: status of the new faculty members (Albers: “visiting” appointments, against “this constant over-democratic nonsense”)
Dreier to Edward Dahlberg (Dahlberg's reply on August 24; Dahlberg to Albers on the 28th; Corkran to Dahlberg on the 29th; Kenneth Murdock to Corkran, August 6 and 30, 1948: “eccentric”)

Faculty meetings (August 27 and 28) and Board meeting (August 27): Rondthaler resigns as treasurer; Dreier gives up the rectorship; Dehn proposes Albers, elected rector unopposed; a “spirited and inconclusive” discussion on new “visiting” faculty without a vote for two years; a pledged gift of 2,000 dollars; plans for a large art institute the following summer

Faculty meeting: no more dietitian, maintenance man, administrator, bookkeeper or secretary; Charlotte Schlesinger and Ray Trayer elected to the Board for a quorum; a revised course list sent to students with the option of a refund

Special meeting of the Board: Max Dehn (now at the University of Wisconsin) will come once a month for a seminar in mathematics and philosophy; Ray Trayer, “The Farmer and Society”; Pete and Betty Jennerjahn promoted to faculty rank (printing, eurythmics)
Mervin Lane's handwritten recollections of BMC (“really living her ideas”)
Albers to the Hansgirgs (Hazel Larsen's negatives); Albers to Olson, Sept. 24, 1948

Less than two weeks after arriving, Dahlberg tells Albers he can no longer stand the college and leaves the same day; the students attribute it to an advance rebuffed by Natasha Goldowski at a party with wine and waltzes
Albers to Milton Rose: two Australian architects plan a rammed-earth studio (600-700 dollars), never built
Albers to Milton Rose (Whitney Foundation): a concentration on the arts and music, about 15 faculty members, professional administrators, “the development of will”

Late September, a fire destroys Natasha Goldowski's laboratory (and the darkroom where Hazel Larsen had stored her negatives); buckets of water from the bathtubs; the Black Mountain fire department does not respond; a building valued at 12,000 dollars, insured for less than 2,000
Telegram from Charles Olson to Albers, recommended by Dahlberg: he will come three days a month (travel expenses and 120 dollars)
Faculty meeting: Natasha Goldowski's new seminar (Our Destinies and Our Instincts)
Faculty meeting (resumed): Albers tries to expel two non-art students found together at night in the Studies Building (they stay); Goldowski asks what the college's principles are
Faculty meeting: Albers proposes an outside governing body (a Board of Trustees); Molly Gregory: better to close “than sell their birthright”
Albers to Mrs. S. A. Bauer (reorganization)
Albers to Dr. Samuel Cooley: composition of the future Board of Trustees (six outsiders, three faculty members: Albers, Dreier, Charlotte Schlesinger)
Board of Fellows meetings (December 1 and 6, 1948) on the pension fund

Meeting at the college of the six prospective trustees: Mrs. Graham Blaine, John E. Burchard (MIT), Beaumont Newhall, Bartlett H. Hayes Jr., Dr. Samuel Cooley, Alex Reed; suggestions: fees at 1,800 dollars, a loan fund, aid capped at 900, a loan on the property, arts-music-writing, publicity, alumni
Milton Rose to Albers: the Whitney Foundation will not fund BMC in 1949
“Tentative Program for 1949–1950” (tuition, scholarships)

Meeting at Mrs. Graham Blaine's in New York: Dreier decides to stay; signs of hope (food prices down 20 %, N. O. Pittenger, former treasurer of Swarthmore, approached as administrator, a work camp planned to build a laboratory, gravel rights sold to the Grove Stone and Gravel Company); Newhall, Burchard and Blaine decline to be trustees; idea of a “Board of Visitors”; plan to rename the college “Black Mountain College of the Arts”

Five faculty members (Nell Rice, Natasha Goldowski, Erwin Bodky, Frank Rice, Ray Trayer), a bare majority, ask for Dreier's resignation; Nell Rice tells him on the day of his return; a petition by the majority of the students
Special faculty meeting: Ray Trayer's statement read by the secretary (Dreier's appeal raising the prospect of closing before the second term)
Dahlberg to Albers: “You never answer my letters”
Resignations of Dreier (from the Board), Josef and Anni Albers, Trude Guermonprez and Charlotte Schlesinger; Albers to the Advisory Council; Gropius leaves the Advisory Board shortly afterward
Pittenger to Trayer; Trayer to Frank Aydelotte (February 23 and 28, 1949); Dehn to Albers (Feb. 23) and Goldowski to Albers (March 24) to keep them

Faculty meeting: Natasha Goldowski, secretary, looks for new faculty (advised by Pittenger and Frank Aydelotte, Nell Rice's brother); Ray Trayer acting rector; Buckminster Fuller agrees to direct the summer session
Albers to the faculty (petition for a special meeting calling for Dreier's resignation)
Goldowski to Fuller (March 16 and 31), Fuller to Goldowski (March 22, 1949): Fuller accepts 800 dollars for six weeks (his rate is 1,000 dollars a month)
Pittenger to Trayer (March 25 and 30, 1949) on the sale of the gravel land and Forbes's mortgage

Kenneth Rexroth (at Olson's suggestion) asks Levi for a position; a long exchange with Goldowski (April 21, May 4, May 13, June 9, August 6 and 9, 1949…): invited for the summer, the fall, the year, then without salary; Rexroth (Guggenheim, an offer from Bennington) finally proposes the spring of 1950, refused for lack of money
Ted Dreier leaves Black Mountain for good in mid-April 1949; with Bobbie Dreier in Florida, then camping in the West
Official letter from the new Board of Fellows to the “Friends of the college” (property valued at nearly 200,000 dollars; self-supporting from 1946 to 1948)
Dreier's fifteen-page mimeographed “Report” to the Advisory Council and friends of the college (“serious trouble… giving new people power too soon”)
Trayer to Pittenger: the idea of recalling John Andrew Rice (Harper centenary prize for his autobiography); Pittenger (May 28), on Aydelotte's behalf: a bad idea
Dreier to Dr. Samuel Cooley (pension); Dreier to Forbes, June 12, 1949
Fuller's three-page “Outline” (“Man has now completed the plumbing…”); Olson to Goldowski (June 1) and her reply (June 11, 1949)
Faculty meeting; Trayer to the faculty

Goldowski to Jerry Wolpert (a former student): no position for the year; Wolpert, who had resigned his job, replies on July 8 (“your fraudulent college”); Goldowski's reply on July 13; Wolpert dies of polio a few days after his letter
Trayer to Pittenger: a plan to take in dissident faculty and students from Olivet College; only Paul Leser (anthropologist) and Flola Shepard (linguist) come
Death of Jerry Wolpert, a former student, from polio
Faculty meetings (July 18, Sept. 5, Oct. 28, 1949) on hiring
Goldowski to Dehn (a suggestion to take Charlotte Schlesinger back, not followed up)
Special faculty meeting: sale of 70 acres to the Grove Stone Company for 30,000 dollars (less a 10 % commission), negotiated up by Pittenger from 22,500; other neighbors had only leased their rights
Dreier to Pittenger: suspending the Alberses' annuities is “a breach of faith”; Pittenger's reply, Sept. 27, 1949 (“having practically wrecked the boat”)
Goldowski to the Rondthalers: “I have great hopes that next year will be a success”
Pittenger to Dreier (pension); Johanna Jalowetz to the Board, May 20, 1950

Faculty meetings (Sept. 29, Oct. 4, 11, 14, 16, 30, 1949) on an outside Board and the rectorship: Levi (“Black Mountain functions much more as a family than as an institution”), M. C. Richards, Dehn, the Jennerjahns, Leser (the example of Olivet) against Trayer and Corkran
Pittenger announces his resignation as rector (end of the fall)

Invitations for the summer of 1950: Hemingway (Goldowski), de Kooning (Levi: “vibrations considerably less negative”), Schlesinger Jr., W. C. Williams, Trilling, Goodman, Kazin, Tobey, Gwathmey, Pollock, Greenberg, Gottlieb, Tanguy, Rothko, Knaths, Maciver, Stamos, Shahn, Pereira
Board meeting; faculty meeting of Nov. 25, 1949 (Dehn: “German students who, facing… 1933, said that they needed a dictator”)
Forbes to the Board: the search for a rector at 90 dollars a month; proposes the title of “president”; fails in the spring and leaves for Europe

Faculty meeting: Student Moderator Nick Cernovich's student poll in favor of reappointing M. C. Richards, Levi and Fiore, whom the Board (8 of the 22 faculty members, by secret ballot) had refused to renew
The faculty votes in favor of M. C. Richards and Fiore; Richards reinstated; Flola Shepard asked to speak to Fiore about the “irregularity” of his life
Board meetings (May 10; June 1, 2, 7, 8, 1950): deadlock over Levi's reappointment, motions to reconsider by Corkran, Trayer and Warrington
Report of the “fact-finding committee” (Goldowski, Hetherington, the students Vera Williams and Andy Oates) summarizing the two positions
Faculty compromise (June 8 and 14): a rector appointed for three years, not a teacher; Levi's reappointment secured
Corkran resigns as registrar and from the Board (“no longer representative of the opinions and forces dominating the college”)
At the end of June, the rectorship is offered to Richard Ballou (Ethical Culture schools); Wesley Huss (a Quaker, Hedgerow Theater) hired as administrator and drama teacher after five visits

Albers to the BMC treasurer (2,000 feet of yellow-pine flooring left to the college; Warrington to Albers, Dec. 2, 1949); Albers claims the remaining 20 % of the pension (Board, Feb. 22, 1950?); letter of Nov. 2, 1950: no longer to be mentioned in the college's publications; Albers to the Board, Jan. 17, 1952
Ballou declines the rectorship (“confusion” between community and education)
Huss to Paul Williams (Jan. 5, May 26, 1951) and to Steinau (Jan. 27, 1951): Paul Williams's last-minute checks

Mary Caroline Richards to Olson (April 13, May 18, June 11, 1951; Olson's replies April 23, May 19): she offers him her apartment and her board for the summer; Mary Fitton and Joel Oppenheimer collect 100 dollars from the students
Early 1951, new efforts to attract Black students; M. C. Richards to Oakley C. Johnson (August 8, 1951), whose reply of August 11 objects to the lowercase in “Negro”

Faculty meetings on the “educational aims” (Oct. 25, Nov. 2, 9, 21, 28, 30, 1951): Olson against Adams and Sprague (“this place goes blind”; “the absolute freedom of the student”); Huss: Olson “not so hot as administrator”

Huss to Forbes (Jan. 16, March 12, 1952): a review (Doyle Jones's farm, Paul Williams's loans of 5,000 dollars for the herd and 5,000 for scholarships, the science building finished by Dan Rice, sale of five acres, accreditation, the Community Council revived); Forbes declines (Jan. 20, 1952; he has given more than 20,000 dollars in all)
Marguerite Wildenhain to Olson (March 5) and Olson to Wildenhain (March 8, 1952) on craft and education; Olson to Wildenhain [1952] on the program of “institutes”
“Report of the Work Committee to the Faculty”; Len Billing (a student in the 1930s) returns to supervise the work program; nine work scholarships (up to 30 hours a week)
Faculty meetings (Nov. 21, 28, 1951; Jan. 18, 24, July 9, Oct. 7, 1952) and Board meetings (Oct. 14, 1952: “Agreed that Mr. Olson should be reminded of his responsibilities”; Nov. 29, 1952)

Ten-day pottery institute: Bernard Leach, Shoji Hamada, Soetsu Yanagi, Marguerite Wildenhain (“host potter”); Hamada sets to work with the local clay and sells his pots for 2 or 3 dollars; local potters enroll (800 dollars recovered)
After Thanksgiving dinner, members of the community put their turkey bones in Karen Karnes's dishes as a sign of contempt (recollection of Remy Charlip)
Board meeting: Paul Williams takes a separate mortgage on the farm of up to 25,000 dollars; vegetable gardens, a tobacco barn
Olson to the Board; Rondthaler to Huss (April 12, 1953); Huss to the Rondthalers (Sept. 30, 1953)
John Michael Schram to the Rockefeller Foundation (work scholarships); Schram, interviewed by Wolpe at the Automat on 57th Street, visits the college for two days (“a company convent”)
Logging and a sawmill: the dogwood forest cut for a shuttle maker who refuses the lot; Hazel-Frieda Larsen to Paul Williams on the pines
Paul Taylor at BMC; Constance Olson to Taylor (June 9, 1953)
First performance of Cunningham's “Banjo,” with Viola Farber and Paul Taylor
Huss to Dr. James Hillman (North Carolina College Conference): BMC stops paying the 21-dollar dues; end of the quest for accreditation

Forbes to R. R. Williams (Dec. 7), the reply (Dec. 8), Forbes to Huss (Dec. 18); Huss to Forbes (Dec. 4 and 21, 1953, Jan. 27 and March 26, 1954): checking the mortgage interest, a 1,000-dollar note deferred
Fannie Allen to the Forbeses: rumors of closing
A new, purely nominal Advisory Council: Albert Einstein (statement of Jan. 16, 1954), Franz Kline, Carl O. Sauer, Norbert Wiener, William Carlos Williams
Karl Heiser to the faculty (a center for disturbed children; Huss's reply, April 14, 1954: the college still exists)
Board meeting: visits and warnings from the health inspectors (the Studies Building sewer polluting the lake)

Olson to Gilmore Johnson (May 6, 21, June 30, August 6, 1954) for approval for Korean War veterans; replies (July 21, Sept. 8, 1954; April 4, May 28, 1956); a V.A. inspection (the same students in disguise from class to class); approval granted, then withdrawn
Olson to “All Those Who Care About BMC”

Forbes–Olson correspondence (Jan. 12, 15, 20, 29, Feb. 19, March 8, 1955) and Nell Rice–Forbes (Jan. 13, April 15, 22, 1955): Forbes refuses any partial sale and wants a sale of the whole (debts: about 45,000 dollars in salary arrears, about 40,000 to Paul Williams)
Forbes to Nell Rice (April 6), to Roy A. Taylor (April 27); Forbes to Olson (May 9, 1955): the notes fall due on June 29, failing which foreclosure
Creeley to Alexander Trocchi: a request for texts (a story by Beckett)

Mary Fiore raises 5,250 dollars from her family; Huss informs Forbes that the sum is in escrow (May 26); Forbes's reply (May 28, 1955): “I simply do not have the faith in Charles Olson that I have had in previous Rectors”; foreclosure averted before the June 29 deadline
Deadline set by Forbes for the mortgage notes: without payment, foreclosure (paid thanks to Mary Fiore)
Meeting (April 13, 1956, then Sept. 27, 1956); in the spring of 1956 the lower campus is rented to a Christian boys' camp (opened in the summer of 1956), which its operator then decides to buy
Premiere of Robert Duncan's Medea (second performance on August 30, 1956)
Second and last performance of Robert Duncan's Medea at Black Mountain
